newsitem.title: DUBAI: Qatar denies its nationals in Bahrain spy ring.
newsitem.headline: Qatar denies its nationals in Bahrain spy ring.

text.p: Qatar denied on Monday that two Qataris that Bahrain said it had arrested were spies.
"An interior ministry official source completely denied Bahrain's statement... about the involvement of two Qatari nationals in a spying operation for Qatar," the official Qatar New Agency reported.

It said the source "expressed his surprise over the statement which was issued a few days before the convening of a Gulf Arab summit in Doha at a time when Qatar is exerting sincere efforts to host this important event... ."
Bahrain said on Monday it had arrested a man and a woman from neighbouring Qatar on charges of spying.
A government official quoted by the Gulf News Agency said Bahrain's security forces had arrested the pair and "they confessed before an investigating judge to spying for Qatar".
The official named them as Fahad Hamad Abdullah al-Baker and Salwa Jassim Mohammed Fakhri.
The official said they told the judge they were sent to gather information that could "harm Bahrain's state security and passed it to the Qatari intelligence service."
The 28-year-old Baker, who the official described as a Qatari intelligence officer, and his accomplice would be tried in Bahrain.
Fakhri, 33, had also confessed that she was paid by Qatari intelligence for information she passed on, the agency quoted an official source as saying.
The source said Bahrain had arrested a similar group in January 1987 on charges of spying for Qatar.

The Qatar interior ministry source said that Qatar had sent an official memorandum to the Bahraini foreign ministry on November 4 seeking their help in finding al-Baker who had disappeared. His family had failed to trace his whereabouts in Bahrain, the source added.
Qatar sent a similar memorandum to the Bahraini foreign ministry last month enquiring about al-Baker, the source said.
Qatar expressed regret over Bahrain's "provocative statement which is mainly aimed at finding additional ways to disturb brotherly gatherings" between Gulf Arab states, the source said.
The source stressed Qatar's "position of maintaining good relationships" and "non-interference in another country's affairs."
Qatar and Bahrain are locked in a territorial dispute over a group of barren islands, reefs and sandbanks which are strategically important. They have been controlled by Bahrain since the 1930s.
Bahrain said it would boycott the annual Gulf Arab summit due to begin in the Qatari capital Doha on Saturday, saying Qatar had behaved in an "unfriendly" manner.
Bahrain said on Monday it would welcome Qatar's Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani if he had practical ideas for settling the dispute.
